about.title: A city of 1950s yards on **slow ground.**
body: This was a township until 1972, when residents voted to become a city, and it grew up beside Flint as farm fields turned into neighborhoods. Census figures put the typical home here at 1964, and more went up in the 1950s than in any other decade. Many of the lawns, trees and foundation shrubs have had sixty years to settle in, and plenty of those shrubs now reach well past the windows they were planted under.

The ground is slow. The USDA soil survey maps most of the city as Conover loam, which drains somewhat poorly, with wetter Sebewa and Brookston loams in the low spots. Toward the Flint line much of it is mapped as urban land, ground that was cut, filled or built over long ago. Lawns stay soft into spring, and a bed against the house has to send water away from it.

There is a lot of street frontage to keep up, too. The city's Road Division looks after more than 70 miles of major streets and more than 100 miles of local ones, a few still gravel and many draining to ditches instead of curbs. That decides where leaves can go, where snow gets piled and how a mower finishes the front edge of a yard.

points.title: The city plows, locals wait
points.body: Burton's snow plan clears major roads, hills, curves and intersections first and local streets second. After a normal snow the city says local streets take two to three days, so a plowed driveway counts for more than people expect.

points.title: Sidewalks belong to the owner
points.body: The city's road page says the owner or occupant has to clear snow and ice from the sidewalk by 24 hours after a storm ends, and a miss is a municipal civil infraction. We can clear the public walk along with the drive.

points.title: Yard waste goes to EMTERRA
points.body: The city uses EMTERRA for curbside trash, recycling and yard waste. Whatever our crew cuts, rakes or digs goes in our own trailer, so your bags and cans still have room at the curb.

points.title: Burning takes a permit
points.body: The city requires a burn permit, and its code describes an open burning fire as one for brush, tree limbs or garden debris. Check the fire department's rules before lighting a leaf pile, or let a cleanup haul it off.

logistics.title: How we work in Burton.
body: Call or text Rob at [(810) 990-3040](tel:+18109903040), or fill out the [estimate form](/get-an-estimate/). He comes out, walks the yard with you, suggests what it needs and quotes a price. The estimate costs nothing.

The city sits just north of Grand Blanc, about 15 minutes from our shop on Embury Road. Mowing runs on a set day each week, cleanups follow the weather and the ground, and winter service gets set up with Rob before the first snow.

faq.q: Do you do lawn care and snow removal in Burton, MI?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes mows lawns, does spring and fall cleanups, mulches and rebuilds beds, trims shrubs and plows driveways in Burton. We also plow and salt commercial lots and walks. Rob gives free estimates in person.

faq.q: Who plows the streets in Burton?
faq.a: The city's Road Division plows public streets, major roads first and local streets after. The city says locals take two to three days after a normal snow, and longer after a big one. Your driveway and walk are yours to clear, which is where our [snow removal](/snow-removal-burton-mi/) comes in.

faq.q: How do I get rid of yard waste in Burton?
faq.a: The city uses EMTERRA for curbside yard waste, and City Hall at 810-743-1500 can tell you your day and the current rules. Each household can also get one free dump permit a month for a pickup load. When we do a cleanup, we haul everything off ourselves.

faq.q: Can I burn leaves in Burton?
faq.a: Only with a permit, and leaves may not qualify. The fire department issues burn permits, the city code describes open burning as a way to get rid of brush, tree limbs or garden debris, and older city rules said no leaves or grass. Check with the fire department, or have a [fall cleanup](/leaf-removal-burton-mi/) take them away.

faq.q: Why do lawns in Burton stay wet in spring?
faq.a: Most of the city sits on loam that drains slowly, according to the USDA soil survey, and the low spots are wetter still. Heavy mowers on soaked ground can rut and pack it, so we time the first cuts to the ground. If one corner always holds water, ask Rob about [grading](/grading-and-new-lawns/).
